name: appending isn't always O(1)
hook: Appending to an array isn't always O(1). Some appends copy everything.
hook_slide: Appending to an array isn't *always* O(1).
hook_sub: Most appends are one write. A few copy the whole array first.
caption: A list sits on a fixed block of slots. When the block is full, the next append allocates a bigger one and copies every element over: that one append is O(n).
So why is append called O(1)? Because the block doubles. {n} appends trigger only {double_grows} grows and {double_copies} copies in total, about {avg} per append.
Grow by {c} slots at a time instead and the same {n} appends cost {add_copies} copies: {ratio} times more, and it gets worse as n grows.
That's what "O(1) amortized" means: averaged over the run, even though a single append can copy {worst} elements.
Did you know which appends are the slow ones? 👇
cta: Build the whole class from scratch and step through its growth.

slides.h: A list sits on a fixed block
p: Underneath is a plain array, the backing store. Its `capacity` is how many slots it has. Its `length` is how many are used.
The memory after it may belong to something else, so it cannot simply grow in place.
When `length == capacity`, append allocates a bigger block and copies every element over. That one append is O(n).
A geometric series: it sums to under 2n copies across n appends. Spread over n appends, that is O(1) each.
A fixed increment copies again every c appends, re-moving the same early elements. It never escapes O(n) per append.
Amortized means averaged over the whole run. One append can still be O(n).
